title: The Zafarnama's opening
hook: the letter to Aurangzeb begins with praise of God in Persian verse (Zafarnama)

segments.voice: Yesterday, a son's lines for his father: he gave his head, but not his faith. Your line was head, not faith. Where did you hold your principle when letting go was easier? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-one.

The draft sits on the screen. It's to someone who wronged you badly, someone with power. The first line you typed is all heat: how could you. Plenty of people have written that first line and deleted it at two in the morning. Guru Gobind Singh wrote a letter like this to the emperor Aurangzeb. He wrote it in Persian, the language of the emperor's court, in verse. And the first thing he put on the page wasn't the emperor at all.
screen: `THE LETTER TO SOMEONE WITH POWER.` → `ALL HEAT IN THE FIRST LINE.` → `THE GURU'S LETTER BEGINS ELSEWHERE.`

segments.voice: The letter is the Zafarnama. Tradition says it was carried to the emperor by a Sikh messenger, and that it was written in a season of great loss. We'll come to its hard words tomorrow. Today, only its opening. And the opening is praise. In paraphrase, the first lines call on God as perfect in wonders, eternal and generous, the giver of contentment, the provider, the deliverer, the merciful. The Lord who gives without being asked, who holds the earth and the sky, who keeps the whole world fed. Line after line, the names keep coming before a single word goes to the man the letter is for. Notice the language. Persian, and names for God like the Merciful, the Provider, the Generous: names the emperor's own faith also uses. It's the move Akal Ustat made a few days ago: different names, one Lord. The Guru begins the letter on ground the two men share. Notice what the praise does to everything after it. Before any complaint, the letter sets the scene: there is a Judge above both of us, and you and I stand in front of Him. Whatever comes next, a rebuke, a reminder, a demand for honesty, it comes inside that frame. That's not flattery of God to soften the blow. It sets the whole quarrel under Someone greater than either man. And notice the steadiness. Whatever he'd been through, the Guru's first act on the page was to praise. The anger is real, and it's coming. But it doesn't get the first word.
screen: `A LETTER TO THE EMPEROR.` · `IT OPENS WITH THE NAMES OF GOD.` · `SHARED NAMES, SHARED GROUND.` · `A JUDGE ABOVE BOTH OF THEM.` · then, large: `BEGIN WITH PRAISE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: begin a letter with thanks. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one message you need to send: an email you've been dreading, a text to someone you're at odds with, even a note to yourself. Before you think about what you need to say, find what you can begin with. Something you're thankful for, something true and good, something you both stand on. Let that be the first line, inwardly. Then let the rest wait. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
The Zafarnama's opening. The tenth Guru's Persian letter to the emperor begins not with the emperor, but with the names of God: the Generous, the Provider, the Merciful. Today's word.
Your line: begin with praise. Today, open one hard message with a line of thanks before anything else. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-one.

howItsDone: The Zafarnama is included in the Dasam Granth; Sikhs read and recite it in its original Persian and in translation, and its opening is read as praise of God.

original.note: the letter's name, written here in the Persian script it was composed in.

trapdoor: what you thought: a letter to an enemy starts with the grievance.

notes: The opening couplets are paraphrased from memory; please check the list of divine names (perfect in wonders, eternal, generous, giver of contentment, provider, deliverer, merciful) and the 'earth and sky' and 'keeps the world fed' lines.
The messenger is left unnamed and framed as tradition (often given as Bhai Daya Singh); the 'season of great loss' is also framed as tradition, with no events named. Please confirm.
The claim that these names would be familiar from the emperor's own prayers is an interpretive note; please confirm it is fair and respectful to Muslims.
The title is commonly rendered 'epistle of victory'; that gloss was left out under the claims rule. A Keeper may add it.
Original game uses Persian script (the letter's language) rather than Gurmukhi; please check spelling, or swap for ਜ਼ਫ਼ਰਨਾਮਾ.
howItsDone says the opening is 'often sung'; please confirm or trim.
